In his view, [artificial intelligence](https://www.euronews.com/tag/artificial-intelligence) fits in two areas.

item.title: AI @ CLS: Columbia Law School’s Artificial Intelligence Initiative
item.description:
# AI @ CLS: Columbia Law School’s Artificial Intelligence Initiative Launched this fall, the AI Initiative reflects a new approach to preparing lawyers for a profession increasingly shaped by AI.
AI @ CLS: Legal Education and Practice in the Age of AI - YouTube
Tap to unmute
[AI @ CLS: Legal Education and Practice in the Age of AI](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=icrKVIsoFjw) [Columbia Law School](https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCEGWwS9UmNRbt7cK3D5Nt7w)
Columbia Law School7.13K subscribers
[Watch on](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=icrKVIsoFjw)
Artificial intelligence is changing what it means to study and practice law. As AI tools become increasingly embedded into lawyers’ day-to-day work, law students need to develop not only fluency with these emerging technologies, but also the capacity to deploy them responsibly and in service of society at large.
Columbia Law School is meeting this transformative moment. [AI @ CLS](https://www.law.columbia.edu/ai-cls): Columbia Law School’s Artificial Intelligence Initiative, takes a multifaceted approach to AI—equipping students with foundational knowledge, advancing field-defining research, and tackling the profound questions that will define our collective future.
The initiative is grounded in the essential values that constitute the Law School’s unique purpose: open inquiry, academic excellence, and a commitment to preparing students for a rapidly evolving profession.
Moses Professor of Law. “AI presents an extraordinary opportunity to bridge our proud tradition of rigorous, theoretical education with the realities of modern legal practice—to create an environment where students can explore these new tools while developing the judgment, critical thinking, and sense of responsibility to use them well. And, as a law school, we are uniquely positioned to tackle the profound questions AI raises for law, institutions, and society.”
AI @ CLS comprises three interconnected components:
- **Innovating With Purpose**: new courses, curricular modules, hands-on training sessions, and cocurricular programs for students to gain AI skills, develop critical judgment, and embrace a sense of intellectual responsibility for their work. - **Expanding Knowledge**:new faculty members and an ever-growing breadth of AI and law scholarship, fostering exploration of AI’s applications, responsible development, and regulation.
##### Innovating With Purpose In fall 2025, Dean Abebe convened a task force charged with thinking about how to train students to reason carefully and independently, without relying on AI, while equipping them with the AI fluency that they will need to be successful in their careers.
Rather than taking an either-or approach, the policy gives faculty the latitude to make their own determinations about how to use AI in their classrooms and provides clear guidance about how to think about AI in the context of a Columbia Law School education.
The result [is an array of](https://www.law.columbia.edu/areas-of-study/artificial-intelligence-and-technology-law) new courses and curricular modules, hands-on training sessions, and cocurricular programs.
Guha, a computer scientist and legal scholar whose research focuses on AI, provided a framework for understanding different types of AI systems students are likely to encounter at the Law School and in legal practice, as well as an analogy to help students determine which AI tools are best suited for particular tasks.
Going forward, all Columbia Law School students will be able to explore AI through a variety of [curricular options](https://www.law.columbia.edu/academics/courses?level=all&name=&year%5B0%5D=301&start_time=7&end_time=21&area_of_study%5B0%5D=58&evaluation=all&number=&points=any&_triggering_element_name=op&_triggering_element_value=Submit&_drupal_ajax=1), ranging from an introductory lecture course to intensive, subject-specific seminars.
In [Law & AI](https://www.law.columbia.edu/academics/courses/39745), a new upper-level elective survey course co-taught by Gillis and [Eric Talley](https://www.law.columbia.edu/faculty/eric-talley), Marc and Eva Stern Professor of Law and Business, students gain an introduction to the legal, technical, and normative dimensions of artificial intelligence, regardless of their prior background in AI or technical training.
These include such classes as the Law of Artificial Intelligence; Cybersecurity, Data Privacy and Surveillance Law; and Intellectual Property in the Digital Age. Students can also explore AI through experiential learning opportunities, such as the In-House Counsel Tech & Startups externship, and by participating in student organizations and journals that focus on AI and technology.
##### Expanding Knowledge Beyond the classroom experience, AI is reshaping the questions legal scholars ask and tactics they employ to conduct research. Through AI @ CLS, Columbia Law School is supporting and advancing faculty scholarship at the intersection of AI and law while enabling researchers to explore the technology’s applications in legal research, teaching, and practice.
Guha, [who joined the Law School in July](https://www.law.columbia.edu/news/archive/neel-guha-exploring-intersection-law-and-ai), said that, from an institutional perspective, “there’s an opportunity to build our philosophy about AI as a Columbia community,” as well as to develop innovative techniques to “train law students who can effectively negotiate and traverse a professional terrain with this technology.”
Ash’s research focuses on applying computational methods to legal texts.
AI @ CLS also brings together scholars, students, and practitioners to contribute to the development of AI and its responsible application across disciplines.
Faculty are already incorporating AI into their research from a wide range of perspectives, examining how it can be used in legal systems and how the law should respond to AI’s growing reach. Lieff Professor of Law and Vice Dean for Intellectual Life, looking at the [use of artificial intelligence in Chinese courts](https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/2940/); and Wexler examining the implications of [AI in criminal investigations](https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/4798/) and [evidence](https://scholarship.law.columbia.edu/faculty_scholarship/4832/).
To bolster the work of faculty and support students, the Law School is planning a series of events related to AI and the law and offering students additional resources, including access to Harvey and Legora, AI platforms built specifically for the legal profession.

item.title: Mission adopts policy for artificial intelligence usage in city business
item.description:
MISSION — The city council here unanimously adopted **[a policy](https://mccmeetingspublic.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/missiontx-meet-90fb74674c2f46359fb1427abb54b126/ITEM-Attachment-001-d627982b4be24f798deaf959eba182f6.pdf)** regarding artificial intelligence usage in municipal business.
Nonetheless, now that policy is officially adopted through the resolution approved Tuesday, which is meant to establish guidelines for “the responsible, secure, ethical, and lawful use of artificial intelligence.”
State and local governmental bodies are able to implement AI into their everyday operations due to legislation passed during the 89th Texas Legislature session, specifically **[Senate Bill 1964](https://capitol.texas.gov/BillLookup/History.aspx?LegSess=89R&Bill=SB1964)** and **[House Bill 3512](https://capitol.texas.gov/BillLookup/History.aspx?LegSess=89R&Bill=HB3512)**.

Rep. Carra urges Trump to address artificial intelligence threats, raises concerns over data centers
item.description:
Carra urges Trump to address artificial intelligence threats, raises concerns over data centers
Steve Carra called for urgent conversations to ensure that artificial intelligence doesn’t become too powerful to control.
“It doesn’t matter who creates artificial superintelligence (ASI), the whole world is in jeopardy,” Carra said.
Carra believes their warnings should be taken seriously and is critical of branding today’s artificial intelligence as “superintelligence.”
“If artificial intelligence reaches the point of autonomous recursive self-improvement, it would be able to rapidly train itself into being a far superior intelligence, and that intelligence explosion could leave all of us in the dust,” Carra explained.
Carra called for immediate discussions to address the threat of artificial intelligence and cautioned against hyperscale data centers, which have emerged as a key concern in Michigan.
